frictionVectors.title: EU Energy Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: European dependence on Algerian gas gives Algiers leverage, but pricing, supply commitments, and emissions rules constrain its room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Southern Border Instability
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Libya, Mali, and Niger increases border-security costs and creates pressure for deeper external intelligence and security partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: China remains central to major transport and public-works financing, creating long-term exposure to repayment terms, contractors, and strategic access.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Revenue Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon dependence leaves sovereign fiscal capacity vulnerable to price cycles and preserves substantial influence for foreign operators and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou's trade role links Benin's growth to foreign logistics firms, regional transit politics, and infrastructure financing conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity near the Burkina Faso and Niger frontiers is increasing security demands and may expand reliance on external training, intelligence, and equipment.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond Market Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains strong leverage over diamond policy, but dependence on global demand and major international trading networks limits full autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Power Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on regional electricity imports and scarce water resources creates infrastructure vulnerabilities that can invite external capital and technical influence.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The shift away from Western military partners toward Russian-linked security support increases room for diplomatic autonomy but creates new dependency risks.

frictionVectors.title: Informal Gold Control
frictionVectors.details: Artisanal production, smuggling, and insecurity limit state capture of gold revenues while exposing the sector to opaque regional and foreign networks.

highlights: Nickel and gold ambitions under tight fiscal pressure
Regional diplomacy strained by Rwanda and eastern DRC tensions

frictionVectors.title: MINING GOVERNANCE AND TRACEABILITY
frictionVectors.details: Gold and emerging nickel projects attract foreign capital while weak oversight and informal production limit Burundi’s ability to capture full value. Export transparency and local processing remain major sovereignty gaps.

frictionVectors.title: GREAT LAKES SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain volatile over alleged support for armed groups in eastern DRC. Cross-border insecurity risks diverting state resources and increasing dependence on external security partners.

highlights: Stable maritime hub with expanding blue-economy ambitions
Tourism and connectivity remain externally financed

frictionVectors.title: MARITIME RESOURCE CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and limited surveillance capacity constrain Cabo Verde’s control over its exclusive economic zone. Port, satellite, and coast-guard partnerships are strategically valuable but create dependence on outside providers.

frictionVectors.title: INFRASTRUCTURE AND DEBT EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Airports, ports, tourism, and digital infrastructure rely heavily on foreign investment and concessional finance. The government retains strong institutional leverage, but external shocks can narrow policy autonomy.

highlights: Oil, gas, timber, and mining remain core sovereignty tests
Anglophone conflict continues to weaken national cohesion

frictionVectors.title: RESOURCE AND INFRASTRUCTURE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign firms are deeply involved in roads, energy, mining, and extractive supply chains. Cameroon gains infrastructure but faces persistent concerns over opaque contracts, limited local processing, and uneven revenue capture.

frictionVectors.title: ANGLOPHONE CONFLICT
frictionVectors.details: Separatist violence in the Northwest and Southwest disrupts transport, agriculture, and public administration. Insecurity reduces the state’s practical control over territory and complicates major infrastructure projects.

highlights: Russian security partnership dominates strategic space
Gold and diamond wealth remains largely outside effective state control

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY AND MINING ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: The government relies heavily on Russian-linked security assistance while granting or tolerating privileged access to mining zones and political influence. This arrangement strengthens regime survival but narrows independent control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: FRAGMENTED TERRITORIAL CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups, illicit gold and diamond networks, and weak transport infrastructure limit Bangui’s reach beyond major urban centers. Regional instability and cross-border trafficking continue to undermine formal resource governance.

highlights: Post-transition government seeks autonomy after French military exit
Oil revenues face security, governance, and regional pressures

frictionVectors.title: OIL DEPENDENCE AND REVENUE CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon income remains central to state financing, but limited diversification and opaque revenue management constrain sovereign development. Foreign operators retain substantial technical and commercial leverage over production and export systems.

frictionVectors.title: SAHEL AND SUDAN SECURITY ARC
frictionVectors.details: The war in Sudan, armed-group activity, and border insecurity impose heavy costs on Chad and drive demand for external security partnerships. N'Djamena is balancing post-French strategic autonomy with ties to Gulf, Russian, and regional actors.

frictionVectors.title: France and Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France's control of Mayotte remains the central sovereignty dispute, limiting Comoros' effective authority over surrounding waters and migration policy.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port, energy, and connectivity projects depend heavily on foreign financing, leaving Moroni with limited bargaining power over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and Regional Intervention
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the east continues to undermine Kinshasa's territorial control, while alleged external support networks around M23 intensify regional sovereignty disputes.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Contract Asymmetry
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and Western competition for cobalt, copper, and other strategic minerals brings investment but leaves the state exposed to opaque contracts, weak oversight, and limited local value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Foreign oil companies remain central to production and technical capacity, while dependence on hydrocarbons restricts fiscal and strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed roads, ports, and public works expand connectivity but increase concerns over debt terms, procurement transparency, and long-term control of strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Cocoa Value
frictionVectors.details: Cote d'Ivoire has strengthened regulation and processing ambitions, but multinational traders and processors still capture substantial value from its dominant cocoa sector.

frictionVectors.title: Northern Security and Connectivity
frictionVectors.details: Militant spillover from the Sahel pressures border security and transport spending, increasing reliance on foreign security cooperation and infrastructure finance.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Footprint
frictionVectors.details: US, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities generate revenue and leverage but constrain Djibouti's strategic autonomy and expose it to great-power rivalry.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Debt Dependence
frictionVectors.details: China-linked port and rail projects underpin the economy while debt exposure and Ethiopia's reliance on Djibouti's corridor create persistent sovereignty and bargaining risks.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf and IMF financial dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gulf investment and IMF-backed financing support Egypt's balance of payments but increase external influence over strategic assets and economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Nile dam confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved dispute with Ethiopia over GERD operations continues to threaten Egypt's water security, with diplomacy producing limited enforceable guarantees.

frictionVectors.title: Declining oil and gas output
frictionVectors.details: Maturing fields and dependence on foreign technical and financial partners constrain domestic control over an increasingly difficult hydrocarbon sector.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque infrastructure partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and maritime projects expand state capacity but deepen creditor, contractor, and strategic dependence on external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector concentration
frictionVectors.details: Gold, copper, and zinc projects rely heavily on foreign capital and expertise, creating persistent questions about revenue transparency and long-term domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea regional militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's location near shipping routes and conflict zones draws competing external security interests while its relations with Ethiopia and neighboring states remain volatile.

frictionVectors.title: South African economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade, transport, energy, and financial links with South Africa provide essential access but leave Eswatini vulnerable to regional policy shifts and supply disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar and textile exposure
frictionVectors.details: Export earnings depend on preferential market access and foreign-linked agribusiness and manufacturing investors, limiting sovereign control over value chains.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: The dam expands Ethiopia's control over electricity generation and regional exports, but unresolved tensions with Egypt and Sudan keep water infrastructure geopolitically exposed.

frictionVectors.title: Debt restructuring and external finance
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressure and reliance on international financial support limit policy space, while conflict-related instability threatens transport, telecom, and energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining influence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign operators remain central to manganese and mineral logistics, limiting Libreville's control over downstream value. The government is seeking more local processing and stronger state participation.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: External creditors and operators retain influence over major transport and port infrastructure. Fiscal pressure constrains the transitional government's ability to renegotiate concessions quickly.

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for trade routes, food supply, energy links, and regional security. This provides resilience but narrows Banjul's room for independent infrastructure and commercial policy.

frictionVectors.title: Fragile port and energy base
frictionVectors.details: Limited electricity generation, shallow logistics capacity, and dependence on donor-backed projects restrict sovereign control over economic infrastructure. Tourism and remittances remain vulnerable to external shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal gold mining
frictionVectors.details: Galamsey continues to damage water systems, farmland, and state legitimacy while diverting mineral value from formal channels. Enforcement is politically sensitive because mining supports livelihoods in several regions.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-mineral bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Accra is seeking greater local value capture in gold, lithium, and bauxite, but financing needs and investor pressure limit its negotiating space. IMF-linked fiscal constraints further narrow options for state-led industrial expansion.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of Simandou
frictionVectors.details: Rio Tinto, Chinalco, and the Winning consortium dominate the capital, technology, and logistics required to develop the iron-ore corridor. Guinea's state seeks infrastructure and revenue gains but remains exposed to partner-controlled financing and execution.

frictionVectors.title: Military transition uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: The junta's political timetable and institutional opacity increase uncertainty over contracts, taxation, and local-content rules. Mineral wealth is being used to strengthen regime legitimacy without a fully accountable civilian framework.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Guinea-Bissau exports most cashews with limited domestic processing, leaving farmers and state revenues exposed to foreign buyers and volatile prices. Weak logistics and finance prevent meaningful downstream sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Bissau port competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, road, and trade interests compete for access to the country's narrow economic base, while political instability weakens regulatory oversight. Security concerns and allegations of illicit trafficking further erode state control.

highlights: Ports and Power as Strategic Assets

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is seeking to rebalance financing relationships around major transport and energy projects while managing repayment pressure linked to Chinese-backed infrastructure. This limits Nairobi's room to set purely domestic priorities for strategic corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu Corridor Contestation
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu port and associated transport corridor remain vulnerable to local opposition, insecurity, and uneven commercial demand. External investors and regional partners continue to influence the pace and design of the project.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water transfers to South Africa provide vital revenue but also create structural dependence on Pretoria for infrastructure, market access, and project security. Delays and cost pressures can reduce Lesotho's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and Mining Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's export base remains exposed to foreign buyers, preferential trade regimes, and externally owned production. Limited domestic processing leaves the country vulnerable to decisions made outside its borders.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, gold, and other mineral projects are central to growth but are largely dependent on foreign capital, technical capacity, and export logistics. Weak domestic value addition leaves Liberia exposed to unfavorable revenue and employment outcomes.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators and investors retain influence over major port and transport infrastructure. This creates recurring sovereignty concerns over tariff-setting, concession terms, and control of mineral export routes.

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Libya's National Oil Corporation and export infrastructure remain vulnerable to rival political and armed factions. Repeated blockades and disputes over revenue allocation prevent stable sovereign management of the country's principal resource.

frictionVectors.title: Proxy Infrastructure Competition
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, Egypt, the UAE, and European states retain significant influence through security partnerships, bases, energy interests, and migration arrangements. External leverage reinforces Libya's fragmented authority over ports, borders, and energy corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mining Chains
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects attract substantial overseas capital but generate limited domestic processing and bargaining power. Commodity-price swings and foreign offtake arrangements constrain Madagascar's ability to capture more value.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Transport Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable electricity and weak transport links increase reliance on external financiers and operators for strategic infrastructure. This dependence can narrow policy autonomy while delaying broader industrial development.

highlights: Debt restructuring tied to IMF discipline

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-backed reforms limit policy space, while shortages of foreign exchange constrain fuel, fertilizer, and infrastructure imports.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector governance
frictionVectors.details: Uranium, rare-earth, and other mineral projects attract foreign capital, but weak regulatory capacity creates risks of limited domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector confrontation
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are pressing foreign mining operators for larger state participation and revenue shares, increasing legal and operational uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: Security dependence on Russia
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian security support has expanded as relations with Western partners deteriorate, while insecurity continues to threaten transport corridors and mining zones.

frictionVectors.title: GTA gas-project dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal offers major export potential but exposes Mauritania to cross-border coordination, financing, and price risks.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of extractive infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and energy logistics remain dependent on international operators and external capital, limiting domestic processing and bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos transition arrangements
frictionVectors.details: The sovereignty settlement over the Chagos Archipelago, including the Diego Garcia base, requires careful management of security, financial, and bilateral commitments.

frictionVectors.title: External dependence in food and energy
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius retains strong institutional control but remains exposed to imported fuel, food, and shipping costs because of its island geography.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara contestation
frictionVectors.details: Control and development of Western Sahara underpin Morocco's resource and infrastructure strategy but continue to generate diplomatic and legal friction.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign capital in strategic sectors
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf, Chinese, and other investors support ports, renewables, logistics, and industry, creating leverage opportunities alongside exposure to external priorities.

highlights: LNG Restart Still Hinges on Cabo Delgado Security
Rwanda and SADC Sustain Counterinsurgency Support

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Militant attacks continue to threaten LNG infrastructure and constrain state authority in the resource-rich north. Foreign security assistance remains essential, limiting Maputo's operational autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: LNG Contractual Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Multinational LNG operators control much of the capital, technology, and export architecture. Delays and renegotiation risks continue to expose Mozambique to external leverage.

highlights: Green Hydrogen Ambitions Attract External Capital

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Ownership Terms
frictionVectors.details: Offshore oil discoveries are increasing pressure to secure stronger local participation, taxation, and environmental safeguards from international operators.

frictionVectors.title: Export Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Green hydrogen and oil development depend on foreign finance, ports, specialized technology, and regional logistics. Windhoek retains policy leverage but faces competition among external investors.

highlights: Junta Reasserts Control Over Uranium and Oil
Benin Pipeline Dispute Threatens Export Capacity

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The military government is seeking greater state control and better terms in uranium and other extractive sectors, increasing tensions with established foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Regional Isolation
frictionVectors.details: Political rupture with Benin has complicated crude exports through the coastal pipeline. Sanctions legacies, border insecurity, and reduced Western support continue to constrain infrastructure sovereignty.

highlights: Oil Reform Meets Persistent Theft and Sabotage

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Production Control
frictionVectors.details: International firms remain important to offshore production, financing, and technical capacity, while fiscal dependence on hydrocarbons limits Abuja's negotiating room.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Oil theft, vandalism, and militant activity continue to reduce government revenue and undermine reliable control of producing regions. Security partnerships and private operators remain necessary.

highlights: Mineral Processing Ambitions Meet Conflict Scrutiny

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Mineral Networks
frictionVectors.details: Kigali faces persistent international accusations that regional security operations and commercial networks facilitate access to eastern Congolese minerals. Diplomatic pressure threatens Rwanda's investment and aid relationships.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's regional influence relies on disciplined security forces and external military, development, and investment partnerships. Escalation with the DRC could trigger sanctions or reduce strategic autonomy.

highlights: Gulf of Guinea security partnerships deepen

frictionVectors.title: UNPROVEN HYDROCARBON FRONTIER
frictionVectors.details: International operators retain interest in São Tomé and Príncipe's offshore blocks, but commercial discoveries remain unproven. Exploration terms and limited state capacity create risks of external leverage before revenues materialize.

frictionVectors.title: MARITIME SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The country relies heavily on foreign partners and regional initiatives to monitor its maritime zone and protect potential offshore assets. This improves security but limits autonomous control over its waters.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN ENERGY CONSORTIA
frictionVectors.details: Gas and oil projects led by BP, Kosmos Energy, Woodside and partners are expanding state revenues but leave Senegal dependent on foreign capital, technology and marketing networks. The government is pressing for greater transparency, local processing and domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: RESOURCE NATIONALISM AND CONTRACT REVIEW
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are reviewing mining and energy contracts to increase the public share and strengthen sovereignty over strategic assets. Abrupt changes could create disputes with investors and delay infrastructure development.

highlights: Strategic balancing between India and China

frictionVectors.title: EEZ AND FISHERIES CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles is strengthening surveillance of its vast exclusive economic zone, but limited maritime capacity leaves fisheries and seabed resources vulnerable to foreign exploitation. Partnerships with India and other external powers improve monitoring while raising alignment concerns.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND DEBT LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: The country seeks infrastructure investment without surrendering control of strategic ports or incurring unsustainable debt. Competition among Indian, Chinese and Western partners gives Seychelles bargaining space but requires careful neutrality.

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE AND RUTILE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Sierra Leone's fiscal and export position remains closely tied to foreign-controlled mining operations and volatile commodity prices. Limited domestic processing means much of the value and technical capability remains outside the country.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND RAIL INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed mining, port and logistics projects are reshaping access to mineral corridors. These investments can improve connectivity but may prioritize export routes over broader national industrialization and create long-term concession disputes.

highlights: Maritime sovereignty becomes a national priority

frictionVectors.title: PORT CONCESSIONS AND EXTERNAL RIVALRY
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the Gulf states and other partners compete for influence over ports, logistics and security arrangements. Concessions and bilateral deals can provide vital infrastructure while fragmenting federal authority and limiting unified control of strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE RESOURCES AND MARITIME SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Somalia is asserting rights over offshore oil, gas and fisheries, but piracy, militant activity and weak enforcement restrict effective sovereignty. Foreign exploration and security support remain necessary, increasing the risk that future resource terms favor external actors.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL MINERALS COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, and European partners are competing for influence over South Africa's platinum-group metals, manganese, and battery-mineral value chains. Pretoria is seeking local beneficiation while avoiding alignment that would reduce its strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND RAIL BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Chronic capacity and maintenance problems at Transnet continue to constrain mineral exports and raise dependence on private operators and foreign capital. Reform is progressing, but infrastructure weakness still limits effective sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: SUDAN PIPELINE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan remains dependent on pipelines and export terminals in war-torn Sudan, leaving oil revenues vulnerable to armed disruption and external bargaining. Production and fiscal stability are consequently tied to decisions made beyond Juba's control.

frictionVectors.title: ELITE CONTROL OF OIL REVENUES
frictionVectors.details: Opaque oil accounting, delayed revenue transfers, and patronage politics continue to weaken public control over the country's main resource. International lenders and humanitarian actors have limited leverage over the political distribution of proceeds.

highlights: Gold and ports draw external powers

frictionVectors.title: GOLD WAR ECONOMY
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling remain central to the financing of competing armed networks, with foreign buyers and regional intermediaries shaping access to supply routes. Resource revenues are reinforcing military autonomy rather than state reconstruction.

frictionVectors.title: RED SEA ACCESS CONTEST
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan and prospective Red Sea infrastructure has become strategically important to regional and extra-regional actors. External security, commercial, and diplomatic involvement risks turning infrastructure access into leverage over Sudan's fragmented authorities.

frictionVectors.title: LNG NEGOTIATION PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is attempting to secure greater domestic value, fiscal returns, and local participation in its offshore LNG development while negotiating with international energy companies. Delays reflect a deliberate effort to strengthen state terms without losing investment momentum.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: The expansion of Dar es Salaam and regional rail corridors is attracting interest from Chinese, Gulf, and Western investors. Tanzania is leveraging this competition, but debt, concession terms, and transit dependence remain sovereignty risks.

frictionVectors.title: PORT DEPENDENCE AND FOREIGN CAPITAL
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé strengthens Togo's regional trade leverage but relies on foreign operators, finance, and shipping networks. This creates exposure to external commercial pressure over customs, logistics, and strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: SAHEL MILITANCY SPILLOVER
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence and cross-border trafficking from the Sahel are increasing pressure on northern Togo and diverting state resources from development. International security assistance is useful but may narrow policy autonomy if dependence deepens.

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration and Energy Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: European financial support and migration cooperation give the EU substantial leverage over Tunisian policy. Energy interconnection projects offer investment but may increase long-term external dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate Production Decline
frictionVectors.details: Weak output, labor disputes, and aging infrastructure limit Tunisia's ability to convert phosphate reserves into sovereign fiscal strength.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Sanctions Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The Tilenga and EACOP projects promise export revenue but remain exposed to financing constraints, environmental criticism, and disputes over land and compensation. Foreign operators retain major control over technology, capital, and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Backed Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed transport and power projects improve connectivity while increasing exposure to external creditors and contractual constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: China, the United States, the European Union, and Gulf investors are competing for copper and cobalt access. Zambia is seeking local processing and greater state participation, but financing and technology remain externally concentrated.

frictionVectors.title: Power Supply Constraint
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages and hydropower vulnerability threaten mining output and industrial policy. Emergency imports and private generation reduce immediate stress but raise costs and dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain prominent in lithium, platinum, and other mining investments, providing capital while limiting Zimbabwe's bargaining power over technology, processing, and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Currency and Sanctions Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Currency instability, sanctions, and restricted access to international finance weaken the state's ability to capture and reinvest mineral revenues. Informal trade and opaque licensing further reduce sovereign oversight.
